_slice: County tier round two — the deflator, New York's frozen cap, the township tier, and two abolished county systems
_note: A second Grok round put through the same citation-resolution pass as the first, and the pass again earned its place: it closed one gap open since the first US brief, and refuted one claim outright. Closed: California's school funding cost-of-living adjustment reads BEA's implicit price deflator for state and local government purchases, and the missing piece was never the statute but the table — NIPA Table 1.1.9, line 26, account code A829RD. A federal national-accounts series sets the growth rate of Californian school funding, read once a year at a fixed May 10 date. Refuted: the claim that Houston's charter defines a 'Designated Index' as a named metropolitan CPI. Two City bond Official Statements say only 'inflation'; the phrase appears nowhere. It has been kept out. The county findings converge on one shape. New York caps each county's Medicaid share at its 2015 level and the State absorbs everything above it. California's realignment ratchets against 1991-92 percentages. Pennsylvania townships levy on a roll the county produces. Three states, three mechanisms, and none of them reads a current series — which now looks less like a Californian habit than like what state-to-county money does generally. And the best single document in the pass is about a government that stopped existing in 1960. Connecticut abolished its counties, federal statistics kept reporting on them for sixty-two more years, and a 2022 Federal Register notice finally re-based the American Community Survey, the population estimates and the small area income and poverty estimates onto the state's nine planning regions instead. An abolished tier does not produce migrated financial reports; it produces a statistical geography that outlives the government by six decades.

reports.title: Implicit Price Deflator for State and Local Government Consumption Expenditures and Gross Investment
reports.description: The national accounts price index for what state and local governments buy, published as line 26 of NIPA Table 1.1.9 under BEA account code A829RD, quarterly and seasonally adjusted, on a 2017=100 base. It is the index California names to escalate every school district's base grant — so a federal national-accounts series sets the growth rate of Californian school funding.
reports.cadence_note: The statute names it as the deflator for "State and Local Government Purchases of Goods and Services", which is pre-1991 BEA terminology. The successor series covers consumption expenditures and gross investment together, so the statutory name and the published name have drifted apart without anyone amending either.

release_schedule.note: This specific NIPA underlying-detail price-deflator table (BEA Table 3.9.4-type series) does not have its own standalone release calendar page on bea.gov; it is part of the National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA) table package that BEA republishes/revises alongside every quarterly GDP news release (advance, second, and third estimates), per BEA's official release schedule at https://www.bea.gov/news/schedule. That schedule shows releases roughly monthly (3 per quarter), which is more frequent than the corpus's current releases_per_year=4 (quarterly) figure, but I could not find a page confirming this specific price-index table only updates once per quarter rather than with all three current estimates, so I have not proposed an existing_field_correction. The apps.bea.gov iTable URL on file could not be fetched directly (blocked by robots.txt for automated fetch), but is a standard BEA interactive-table landing page for this series and appears to remain a reasonable, non-dead URL.

reports.title: New York local Medicaid share cap
reports.description: The cap on what each county and New York City contributes to Medicaid. Set in 2005 against each district's calendar-2005 expenditures with declining trend factors, then phased down and frozen: since 2015 a district's local share may not exceed its 2015 level and the State absorbs all non-federal growth above it. A county-level cost driver with no Californian or Texan equivalent, and — like California's realignment — a formula that reads a historical base rather than any current series.

reports.title: County Impact Report on the Executive Budget
reports.publisher: New York State Association of Counties
reports.description: The annual analysis of what the state budget does to county finances, published by the counties' own association. Included because it is the standing published account of the Medicaid cap's effect — the association reports the state takeover saving local districts roughly $8.3 billion in one year.

SFY 2026 Executive Budget County Impact Report

release_schedule.note: NYSAC publishes this report within about a day of the NY Governor's Executive Budget submission, each January. Confirmed instances: SFY2025 report published 2024-01-22, SFY2026 report published 2025-01-22, SFY2027 report published/updated 2026-01-21/22. NY practice (per budget.ny.gov) is that the Governor submits the Executive Budget 'typically by mid-January -- or, following a gubernatorial election year, by February 1.' 2026 is a NY gubernatorial election year, so the SFY2028 Executive Budget (and NYSAC's corresponding impact report) is expected around mid-January to February 1, 2027, rather than the tighter ~Jan 21-22 window seen in non-election-transition years.

reports.title: Pennsylvania Second Class Township Code
reports.description: The 1933 act, reenacted in 1995, under which second class townships levy their own property taxes. Townships are a fourth tier of government this corpus had never modelled — beneath the county and above nothing — and §3205 caps their millage by purpose: fourteen mills for general purposes, three for fire apparatus, half a mill for ambulance and emergency services.

reports.title: Pennsylvania Consolidated County Assessment Law
reports.description: The law making property assessment a county function in Pennsylvania, at 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 88. It is what makes the township tier legible: a township levies on a roll it does not produce and cannot revise.

reports.title: Municipal Annual Financial Report (MunStats)
reports.publisher: Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development
reports.description: The annual financial report every Pennsylvania municipality — city, borough, town and township alike — files with the state, published through the MunStats database. The Pennsylvania counterpart to California's Cities and Counties Annual Reports, and the only place the township tier becomes visible in aggregate.

entries.covers: 2026 municipal annual audit and financial report (boroughs/townships filing deadline)

release_schedule.rule: The Municipal Annual Audit and Financial Report (DCED-CLGS-30) form is due April 1 of each year for Boroughs and Townships. For Cities, the due date is March 1.
release_schedule.note: Deadline is set by statute/DCED form instructions, not a publisher release calendar. Cities file by March 1; Boroughs and Townships (the large majority of PA municipalities) file by April 1 — the April 1 date is used as the representative next occurrence since the 2026-04-01 deadline has already passed relative to today (2026-08-11).

reports.title: Connecticut Public Act 152 of 1959 — abolition of county government
reports.description: The act that ended county government in Connecticut. Since 1960 the state's eight counties "exist only as geographical regions, without their own independent government" — the functions they held, from jails and courthouses to weights and measures, went to the state or to municipalities.

reports.title: Change to County-Equivalents in the State of Connecticut
reports.publisher: US Office of Management and Budget
reports.description: The 2022 Federal Register notice adopting Connecticut's nine planning regions as county-equivalent units for federal statistics, on the ground that the counties "have not served as functional governmental and administrative entities since county government in the state was abolished in 1960". The most interesting single document in the county-tier work: a geography that stopped existing in 1960 kept being reported on for sixty-two years, and this is the instrument that finally stopped it.

reports.title: Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 34B — abolition of county government
reports.description: The chapter abolishing seven county governments between 1997 and 2000 — Middlesex, Hampden, Worcester, Hampshire, Essex, Berkshire and, separately, Franklin — and transferring their functions, employees, assets and liabilities to the Commonwealth. Six counties keep their governments. Included as the partial case beside Connecticut's complete one, and carrying an unusual trigger: abolition comes early if the commissioner of revenue certifies a default on county debt.

reports.title: Texas Local Government Code Chapter 231 — county zoning authority
reports.description: The answer to a question left open in the previous pass. Texas counties have no general zoning power; Chapter 231 grants it only in named places and for named purposes — parts of Padre Island, land around certain lakes, areas near military installations. The absence of a general grant is the structural reason the Texas county tier is so crowded with independent districts.

dependencies.basis: Education Code §42238.02(d)(2): the grade span adjusted base grants "shall be adjusted by the percentage change in the annual average value of the Implicit Price Deflator for State and Local Government Purchases of Goods and Services for the United States, as published by the United States Department of Commerce for the 12-month period ending in the third quarter of the prior fiscal year. This percentage change shall be determined using the latest data available as of May 10 of the preceding fiscal year compared with the annual average value of the same deflator for the 12-month period ending in the third quarter of the second preceding fiscal year." The published series is BEA NIPA Table 1.1.9 line 26, account code A829RD. Open across two research rounds and closed here: the statute was always clear, and what was missing was which table the deflator actually lives in.

reference_period.stated_as: The 12 months ending in the third quarter of the prior fiscal year against the same window a year earlier, both read as of a fixed May 10 date — so the number is frozen two months before the fiscal year it governs begins.

dependencies.basis: The association reports the mechanism directly: "Beginning in January 2006, counties' Medicaid cost contributions were capped based on 2005 expenditures and indexed to a growth rate of 3.5 percent in 2006, 3.25 percent in 2007, and 3 percent per year thereafter." The State Comptroller's own county Medicaid analysis carries the same figures. The report is the standing published account of what the cap costs and saves counties each year.

The code sets both what a township may levy and what it must report. §3205(a) provides that "The board of supervisors may by resolution levy taxes upon all real property within the township made taxable for township purposes, as ascertained by the last adjusted valuation for county purposes, for the purposes and at the rates specified in this section", with fire apparatus "not exceeding 3 mills" and ambulance and emergency medical services "not exceeding 0.5 mill". The code separately requires the township auditors to complete their settlement before April 1 and the secretary to publish concise financial information by April 15, alongside the state filing.

The levy provision reads a roll the township does not produce: taxes are levied on property "as ascertained by the last adjusted valuation for county purposes". Assessment in Pennsylvania is a county function under the Consolidated County Assessment Law at 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 88 — so a township's tax base is set entirely by the county above it, and the township tier has no assessment machinery of its own at all.

reference_period.stated_as: The last adjusted county valuation in force when the township levies.

dependencies.basis: The notice gives the abolition as its reason for acting: the planning regions are adopted as county-equivalents because Connecticut's counties "have not served as functional governmental and administrative entities since county government in the state was abolished in 1960". Sixty-two years between the government ending and the statistical geography following it.

The notice directs the change into named products: the Census Bureau will "adopt the State's nine planning regions as county-equivalent geographic units for purposes of collecting, tabulating, and disseminating statistical data", implemented "internally in 2022, with public data and geospatial products reflecting the change beginning in late 2022. By 2024, all Census Bureau operations and publications." The American Community Survey is named first among the affected programmes.

The notice names "the intercensal Population Estimates Program (PEP)" among the programmes that must re-base onto the planning regions. A county-level estimate for Connecticut published after the transition is an estimate for a different geography than one published before it, which is the kind of discontinuity a graph of dependencies ought to record.

The notice names the "Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE) Program" among the affected products, alongside the Economic Census and County Business Patterns. SAIPE county estimates drive Title I education allocations, so the geography change reaches money.

The county association handout lists the narrow matters on which Texas counties may act by ordinance — subdivision regulation, road and drainage construction, sexually oriented businesses, septic systems, certain flood plain development, and airport zoning — against home rule cities, which "have the constitutional power to adopt any ordinance not in conflict with the constitution or the general laws of the state". Chapter 231 is where the enumerated zoning grants sit, and they are geographic: parts of Padre Island, land around named lakes, areas near military installations.

_dropped.why: Chased hard and refuted. The previous research asserted that Houston's charter defines a "Designated Index" as the CPI-U for the Houston-Galveston-Brazoria metropolitan area. Neither of two City bond Official Statements uses the term "Designated Index" or names any metropolitan CPI; both say only "inflation". A search for the phrase against Houston charter and revenue-cap sources found no instance anywhere. The term appears to be an invention and has been kept out of the corpus. What the Official Statements do confirm is the fiscal 2005 base, the cumulative inflation-plus-population adjustment, the 4.5 percent alternative and the $90 million public safety addition — which is why the two Houston cap edges cite the City's bond disclosure for the formula and the Finance Department budget for the series it reads.

A negative finding that survived a deliberate attempt to break it. No federal allocation formula was found that reads the *count* of local governments as a term — formula factors recur as population, poverty, per capita income, tax effort, housing age and acreage, never a count of units. Even Payments in Lieu of Taxes, which depends on the Census classification of a "unit of general local government", uses acreage and population as its numeric inputs. The closest candidate is the Census Bureau's own internal use of the universe as a benchmark and sampling frame for the annual finance and employment surveys, which is exactly the frame-and-classification use the claim excludes. Recorded as "not refuted" rather than proven, because a negative of this shape cannot be proven by search.

One detail of the cap could not be confirmed, filed as an observation because a caveat has to annotate an edge that exists and this one does not. The research this came from described the 2006-2014 trend factors as non-compounded, and no source reachable states that. The available phrasing ("3 percent of additional growth was permitted") is consistent with a simple base-applied increment but does not establish it. Immaterial to the live mechanism, since the trend factors stopped operating when growth was frozen at 2015 levels, but recorded so nobody later treats the compounding question as settled.

Kept as an island deliberately. Massachusetts abolished seven county governments and kept six, and §4 transferred jails, registries of deeds and courthouses to the Commonwealth — so the abolished counties' reporting obligations moved rather than stopped. Which Commonwealth series absorbed them was not established, and until it is there is no edge to draw. Franklin County's separate 1997 abolition and Suffolk's coterminous status with Boston were both left unverified rather than asserted.

The fourteen-mill general purposes cap is stated in a township supervisors' handbook citing §3205, and the per-purpose caps for fire and ambulance were quoted from a primary reprint. The subsection itself could not be rendered from a primary source: the General Assembly's per-section viewer is robots-blocked and every full-code PDF found truncates before the relevant article. The operative levy clause quoted in the edge above comes from a 2024 amending act that reprints it, which is why the edge cites that act rather than the code.

_dropped.edge: ct-county-abolition-1959 -> a successor county financial series
_dropped.why: The clean answer to the question the corpus was actually asking, and it is two-layered. County *government* financial reporting in Connecticut stopped in 1960 and never acquired a successor — there is no entity to report, and the Census of Governments records no county governments in the state. County *geography* statistical reporting carried on for another sixty-two years on legacy boundaries and was then re-based onto the nine planning regions. So an abolished tier does not produce migrated financial reports; it produces a statistical geography that outlives the government by six decades.
